title: Sample Sort and Count
concept: Test game: pick the move, sort the lines into bins, then build a greeting that pays a stroke debt.
bookIdea: Every person needs recognition from others, and it can come in many forms, good or bad.

opener.setting: Monday, 7:50am. Kesari Heights, flat 3B, the kitchen.

lines.cue: leaning on the counter, mug in both hands

lines.text: “Not really. The neighbours had a party till two.”
lines.cue: not looking up from his phone

opener.ask: Which voice is talking, and what does each line give the other person?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Three quick reads. Listen to the words and the cue together.

items.cue: leaning on the counter, mug in both hands
items.why: She asks a plain question about last night, with nothing copied from anyone and nothing sulky in it. That is the Adult voice.

traps.0: Parent would sound like “You should go to bed earlier, you know.” It passes a rule about bedtime that nobody asked for.
traps.2: Child would sound like “Ugh, I did not sleep either, I hate mornings.” That is a feeling and a complaint, not a question.

items.example:
On a train platform: “Did you get the 7:40 or the 8:05?”
A plain question about what happened, with no advice and no mood in it.

items.text: “I'll take the dishes, you do the bins.”
items.prompt: Which kind of move is this?
items.why: Dana asks for a task and expects the reply to come from the same level. Both people are talking about the flat, so the lines run straight across.

traps.1: Crossed would be a reply like “Why are you always on the dishes?”, which answers a feeling nobody mentioned. The conversation would switch level and stop being about the bins.

items.example:
Team stand-up:
“I'll take the report, you chase the client.”
“Fine, I'll chase them after lunch.”
Each line is answered at the level it was asked.

items.text: “Sorry, sorry, you're right, it's my fault again. I'm hopeless with the bins.”
items.why: The apology is big and the ending is a put-down of himself. It invites Tanvi to reassure him, and the bins never get fixed. That is a game.

traps.0: Ritual would be the same apology said as a set phrase every Monday, with nothing hidden under it.
traps.1: Pastime would be a chat about bins and bin days, with both people enjoying the talk and nothing being won or lost.

items.example:
Family WhatsApp:
“Sorry, I forgot the milk again, I'm useless.”
“Don't be silly, here's the list.”
The second person is now doing the first person's job of reassuring.

items.prompt: Put each line in the right bin.

items.why: A compliment recognises the person, so it is a positive stroke.

items.text: “Can we talk about the bins at seven?”
items.why: Arranging a time is structuring time, not a stroke.
A remark about the weather gives no recognition and no plan.
A greeting is a small stroke, and it is the cheapest one going.

items.example: At the school gate: “Lovely day for it.” A small stroke, given and taken in a moment.

items.prompt: Greet Mr C. He is owed about 10 strokes. Build a greeting that pays them.

palette.text: “Mr C! Back from holiday, I hope?”
“Mr C, the roses on your balcony are wonderful.”

items.underMsg: Under the band. Mr C is still owed some strokes, so he leaves the lift a little cool.
items.overMsg: Over the band. That is more than a greeting, and Mr C can tell he is being handled.
items.hitMsg: In the band. Mr C leaves the lift smiling, and his balance is paid.
items.why: Each line carries a value. The aim is to pay the amount owed, within a small margin, in no more than three lines.

items.text: “So which of those greetings was the warm one, and which one only paid the debt?”
items.prompt: Which word names the warm greeting?
items.why: A warm greeting is a stroke. It recognises the other person, and the count is what the greeting pays out.

traps.1: Trade is the word for a whole exchange, with a request and an answer. A single greeting is one unit, not a deal.
traps.2: Game would mean the greeting hides a second message. Here the greeting says what it says, so nothing is hidden.

items.example:
A neighbour on the stairs: “You're up early, good to see you.”
That is a stroke. Nothing about the stairs or the time is being negotiated.

debrief.meera: Three things to keep. Tanvi's question was a plain Adult question. Vikram's apology was a game with a hook at the end. And a greeting pays its stroke debt when it is warm and short.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a stroke, a unit of recognition that people give and take all day.

reflection.prompt: Think of one stroke you gave or got this week. Did it feel like a plain greeting, or like a payment for something?
